methods.label: Bound what the smaller places can hold
methods.explanation:
The digit restrictions limit how much the smaller factorial places can contribute. This lets us determine larger digits without guessing.

Since \(6!=720>695\) and every summand is nonnegative, every term from \(6!\) onward must be zero. The terms through \(4!\) have maximum total
\[
1+2\cdot2!+3\cdot3!+4\cdot4!=119.
\]
Thus the \(5!\) term must be present. If \(a_5\le4\), the entire sum would be at most
\[
4\cdot120+119=599<695.
\]
Since \(a_5\le5\), we must have \(a_5=5\), leaving \(695-600=95\).

Now write
\[
95=24a_4+T,
\qquad T=a_1+2a_2+6a_3.
\]
The smaller digit bounds give \(0\le T\le1+4+18=23\), so
\[
72\le24a_4\le95<96.
\]
The only possible integer digit is \(a_4=3\). It is achievable, since
\[
695=1+2\cdot2!+3\cdot3!+3\cdot4!+5\cdot5!,
\]
and all these digits satisfy their restrictions. Therefore \(a_4=3\), choice D.

methods.label: Extract the digits by successive division
methods.explanation:
Factorial place values can be grouped in a nested form:
\[
695=a_1+2\bigl(a_2+3\bigl(a_3+4(a_4+5T)\bigr)\bigr),
\]
where \(T\) is an integer collecting the remaining factorial terms.

Because \(0\le a_1<2\), the first digit is the remainder when \(695\) is divided by \(2\). After removing that digit and dividing by \(2\), the next digit is the remainder on division by \(3\), because \(0\le a_2<3\). The same reasoning continues with divisors \(4\) and \(5\).

The divisions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
695&=2\cdot347+1,\\
347&=3\cdot115+2,\\
115&=4\cdot28+3,\\
28&=5\cdot5+3.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the successive remainders are \(a_1=1\), \(a_2=2\), \(a_3=3\), and \(a_4=3\). Each remainder is forced because its permitted digit range is exactly from zero to one less than the divisor.

The remaining quotient \(5\) can be taken as \(a_5=5\), with all higher digits zero. These digits give \(1+4+18+72+600=695\), verifying the representation. Hence \(a_4=3\), choice D.
